cards.title: Composition Over Inheritance
cards.teaser: Favor giving a class a collaborator it owns over making it extend a base class. Composition keeps coupling low, hierarchies shallow, and unit tests easy to write.

runs.text: Inheritance (is-a) couples a subclass to every detail of its parent. When the parent grows a new method, every subclass inherits it whether it wants it or not. When the parent changes internal state, the subclass breaks in ways that are hard to trace. Deep hierarchies — five levels of
— are notoriously hard to read: to understand what
does, you must hold the whole tree in your head at once.
Composition (has-a) avoids this. Instead of subclassing

and call its methods. Any object with the right interface will do — a real logger in production, a fake one in tests, a null object when logging is disabled. The class owns its collaborator without being defined by it.

items.text: when a true is-a relationship exists and you want the child to be substitutable for the parent everywhere (Liskov Substitution Principle).
when you want to reuse behavior without committing to the parent's full interface — especially across unrelated class families.
are the middle ground: small, focused classes that add specific behaviors via multiple inheritance without forming a hierarchy.

runs.text: The Gang of Four (Design Patterns, 1994) codified "favor composition over inheritance" as Principle 1. Python's duck typing makes composition especially natural — you rarely need a shared base class to swap implementations.
Instead of making your class a child of another class, give it a copy of that other class to call. Your class stays independent and you can swap in a different collaborator any time.

cards.title: Abstract Base Classes (ABC)
cards.teaser: ABCs define a contract — a set of methods every subclass must implement. Python raises TypeError at class-definition time if a concrete subclass forgets to implement an abstract method.

This makes ABCs a machine-checked contract. Unlike a docstring that says "subclasses must implement

for structural typing — when you care about method signatures, not class lineage.

runs.text: Register third-party classes that already satisfy your ABC's interface using MyABC.register(ThirdPartyClass) — no subclassing required. isinstance() will then return True for those classes.

An ABC is a checklist baked into the class system. If a subclass skips any required method, Python refuses to create it — you get an error when the class is defined, not when a missing method is called at 2 a.m.

cards.title: Mixin
cards.teaser: A mixin is a small class that provides one focused behavior via multiple inheritance — not a standalone object, not a hierarchy root, just a reusable capability you bolt onto any class that needs it.

runs.text: Multiple inheritance gets a bad reputation, but mixins tame it. A mixin is a class that:

items.text: Implements one cohesive capability (serialization, logging, validation).
— it relies on the concrete class's initializer.
Is never instantiated on its own — it only makes sense combined with a domain class.

runs.text: Because mixins rely only on the interface they expect to find on
(documented by convention or enforced by an ABC), they compose cleanly:
is readable and predictable as long as each mixin stays focused.
Convention: suffix mixin class names with
to signal intent to readers. Keep each mixin under 30 lines. If a mixin is growing, it has taken on too much — split it or promote it to a proper composed collaborator.

Mixins that depend on each other create hidden coupling. If JsonMixin calls ValidationMixin's methods, list both in a class that uses either — and document the dependency. Silent ordering requirements are the primary way mixins become pain.
A mixin is like a USB dongle for a class — plug it in and the class gains a specific new capability without changing what it fundamentally is.

cards.title: @property Decorator
cards.teaser: Turn a method into an attribute that computes its value on access — letting callers use dot notation while the class controls what happens when the attribute is read.

runs.text: In Python, simple attributes are fine to expose directly — there is no Java-style requirement to wrap every field in a getter. But when an attribute's value must be
(derived from other state, formatted, or fetched lazily),
lets you write the computation as a method while giving callers the clean

This is Python's migration path: start with a plain attribute, and if you later need computation or validation, convert to a property without changing any call sites. Callers never know the difference —
looks identical whether it's a stored float or a computed property.

items.text: Keep property getters fast and side-effect-free
— callers expect attribute access to be cheap.
— if the getter makes a network call, use an explicit method instead.
when the computation is expensive and the result is stable.

runs.text: @functools.cached_property (Python 3.8+) computes the value once on first access, then stores it as an instance attribute, bypassing the property descriptor on subsequent reads. It is not thread-safe without a lock.
@property lets a method wear the clothes of a plain attribute. Callers read obj.area with a dot, but behind the scenes Python runs your method and returns what it computes.

cards.title: @property.setter
cards.teaser: A property setter intercepts assignment to a computed attribute, letting the class validate, transform, or synchronize state before storing a new value.

runs.text: alone is read-only — attempting assignment raises
makes the attribute writable while giving the class full control over what happens during assignment.

items.text: if the incoming value is out of range.
— invalidate a cache, fire a callback, or mark the object as dirty when a field changes.

runs.text: Setters that trigger heavy side effects (network calls, database writes) are a design smell. Callers don't expect obj.status = 'active' to make an HTTP request. Prefer an explicit method like activate() for operations with significant consequences.

A property setter is a bouncer on the assignment operator. When code writes obj.speed = 200, the setter runs first — it can reject bad values, transform the input, or update other state before anything gets stored.

cards.title: __init__ vs __new__
cards.teaser: __init__ configures an already-created instance; __new__ creates the instance itself. Nearly all Python code only needs __init__ — __new__ is reserved for singleton patterns, immutable types, and metaclass machinery.

If __new__ returns an instance that is not of type cls, Python skips __init__ entirely. This is a common source of confusion when __new__ returns a cached object.
__new__ builds the house; __init__ furnishes it. You almost always only care about furnishing — leave the building to Python.

cards.title: Class Methods vs Static Methods vs Instance Methods
cards.teaser: Instance methods receive the object; class methods receive the class; static methods receive nothing. Choosing the right kind signals intent and controls what each method can access.

runs.text: Python has three kinds of methods, differentiated by what they receive as their first argument:

items.text: (def f(self, ...)) — the default. Receives the instance as
; can read and write instance and class state.
(@classmethod, def f(cls, ...)) — receives the class as
) and factory methods that must produce the correct subclass.
(@staticmethod, def f(...)) — receives nothing special; a plain function namespaced to the class. Use when the logic is conceptually related to the class but needs neither instance nor class state.

runs.text: Class methods are the Pythonic way to write multiple constructors.
instead of hardcoding the class name means subclasses get the right type automatically.

If you find yourself reaching for a static method that references class-level constants, that's a design signal: maybe those constants belong somewhere else, or the method should become a module-level function.
Instance method: "I need the object." Class method: "I need the class, not a specific object." Static method: "I need neither — I just live here for organizational reasons."

cards.title: super() for Cooperative Multiple Inheritance
cards.teaser: super() delegates a method call to the next class in Python's MRO — not necessarily the parent you'd expect. Using super() consistently makes multiple inheritance safe and predictable.

runs.text: When a class hierarchy uses multiple inheritance, calling
directly is dangerous: it hardcodes the parent, so the method may be called twice (or not at all) when the MRO has a diamond shape.
fixes this by delegating to the next class in the MRO automatically.
to work correctly across a diamond hierarchy, every class in the chain must call
— this is what makes the pattern "cooperative". If one class breaks the chain by calling its parent directly or not calling
at all, classes further along the MRO are silently skipped.

items.text: In Python 3, super() with no arguments
— the class variable is injected by the compiler.
— it's equally important for class methods and properties in a hierarchy.

runs.text: As a rule: always use super() in any class that participates in multiple inheritance, even if you don't think you need it today. Your collaborators' subclasses will thank you.
super() is a relay baton. Every class in the inheritance chain picks it up, does its part, and passes it to the next runner. If anyone drops it, the remaining runners never run.

cards.title: Method Resolution Order (MRO)
cards.teaser: Python's MRO is the linearized order in which classes are searched when looking up a method. It is computed once at class-definition time using the C3 linearization algorithm.

runs.text: In a single-inheritance chain, method lookup is simple: start at the instance's class, walk up to parent, grandparent, and so on until
. With multiple inheritance the order must be unambiguous and consistent — Python uses the
algorithm (also called C3 superclass linearization), which guarantees:

items.text: — a class always comes before its parents.
— the relative order of classes is preserved across all derived classes.
at definition time if no valid linearization exists.

runs.text: Inspect the MRO at runtime with

(a list). Understanding the MRO explains why

Diamond inheritance: if A inherits from B and C, both of which inherit from D, the MRO of A is [A, B, C, D, object]. D's __init__ is called exactly once. This only works if B and C both call super() cooperatively.

The MRO is the ordered list Python uses when looking up a method — it settles "who answers first" for every method call. Check ClassName.__mro__ to see exactly which classes are searched and in what order.

cards.title: __str__ vs __repr__
cards.teaser: __repr__ is for developers — it should be unambiguous and ideally re-creatable. __str__ is for users — it should be readable and friendly. Always define __repr__; define __str__ when the two differ.

runs.text: dataclasses and NamedTuples generate __repr__ automatically. For custom classes, defining __repr__ is the minimum you should always do — it saves enormous time when debugging.

__repr__ tells another developer what the object is, precisely enough to recreate it. __str__ tells a user what the object means, in plain language. If in doubt, define __repr__ — Python will use it as a fallback for everything else.

cards.title: Duck Typing vs Explicit Interfaces
cards.teaser: Duck typing trusts that an object works if it has the right methods — no inheritance required. Explicit interfaces (ABCs, Protocol) add a machine-checked contract when implicit trust is not enough.

runs.text: "If it walks like a duck and quacks like a duck, it's a duck." Python's default is duck typing: you call
and trust the object to have a
check required. This makes Python code flexible —
, and a custom network stream all pass the same "does it have read?" test.

items.text: and a missing one causes a hard-to-diagnose runtime error.
— you cannot inspect every implementation before it runs.
for structural subtyping that mypy checks without forcing inheritance.

runs.text: typing.Protocol (PEP 544, Python 3.8+) is the modern bridge: you define the expected interface as a Protocol class, mypy enforces it statically, but no inheritance is required at runtime. It is structural typing, not nominal typing.

Duck typing says: "I'll just call the method and see." An explicit interface says: "Before we even start, prove to me you have all the methods I need." Python defaults to the former; use the latter when the stakes are high enough to warrant the ceremony.

cards.title: Private Attributes: Single vs Double Underscore
cards.teaser: A single underscore is a social contract: "internal — don't rely on this." A double underscore triggers name mangling: Python renames the attribute to prevent accidental override in subclasses.

runs.text: Python has no true access control — all attributes are technically reachable. Convention and name mangling are its two tools for signaling and enforcing privacy:

items.text: — convention meaning "implementation detail, not part of the public API." Nothing enforces this; callers can still access it. It is also used for "protected" attributes that subclasses may reasonably access.
gets its own mangled name — no collision. Use this to protect attributes that

runs.text: underscores for almost everything. Reach for double underscores only when you have a concrete subclassing-collision problem to solve — not as a blanket "make this private" hammer.
Name mangling is not encryption. Anyone who knows the mangled name (obj._Foo__attr) can still access it. It prevents accidental collisions, not deliberate access.

One underscore is a "keep out" sign that polite callers respect. Two underscores are a fence Python builds automatically — the attribute gets renamed so subclasses can't accidentally stomp on it. Neither is a lock.
